summary: This Wikipedia article describes the 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée on Martinique, a phreatic and Peléan eruption that began 23 April 1902 and ended 5 October 1905. Its climax on 8 May 1902 sent a pyroclastic surge into Saint-Pierre that killed roughly 28,000 people, making it the deadliest eruption of the 20th century. The article also covers the warning signs, the relief efforts led by the United States and others, later fatal eruptions, and the eruption's role in founding modern volcanology.
one_line: Account of the 1902 Mount Pelée eruption on Martinique, which destroyed Saint-Pierre and killed about 29,000 people.
key_facts: The 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée began on 23 April 1902 as a series of phreatic eruptions and ended on 5 October 1905.
The eruption is listed with a VEI of 4 and approximately 29,000 deaths, making it the deadliest eruption of the 20th century.
On 8 May 1902 a pyroclastic surge reached Saint-Pierre at 8:02 a.m., and almost everyone within the city proper, about 28,000 people, died.
The last telegraph transmission from Saint-Pierre at 07:52 on 8 May 1902 was the word "Allez".
The cable repair ship CS Grappler was set on fire and sunk by the surge with the loss of all hands.
The Canadian cargo liner Roraïma was set aflame by the pyroclastic flow, and twenty-eight of her crew and all passengers except two were killed.
Louis-Auguste Cyparis, a felon held in an underground jail cell, was one of the few survivors within Saint-Pierre.
On 5 May 1902 a lahar from the Étang Sec crater buried about 150 people under 60 to 90 metres of mud and generated tsunamis along the coast.

Captain Marina Leboffe of the barque Orsolina left Saint-Pierre with only half of his cargo of sugar loaded, reportedly saying, "I know nothing about Mt. Pelée, but if Vesuvius were looking the way your volcano looks this morning, I'd get out of Naples!"
On 20 May 1902 a second eruption obliterated what was left of Saint-Pierre, killing 2,000 rescuers, engineers, and mariners bringing supplies.
A powerful eruption on 30 August 1902 produced a pyroclastic flow that struck Morne Rouge, killing at least 800 people.
Beginning in October 1902 a lava spine grew in the Étang Sec crater, reaching about 300 m in height and collapsing in March 1903.
On 12 May 1902 US president Theodore Roosevelt instructed the Secretaries of War, Navy, and Treasury to start relief measures at once.
President Roosevelt asked Congress for an immediate appropriation of $500,000 for emergency assistance, and Congress voted $200,000 of immediate assistance.
The study of the disaster marked the beginning of modern volcanology, and Antoine Lacroix was the first to describe the nuée ardente phenomenon.
